title: Taylorsville on Brashears Creek
summary: In 1799 miller Richard Taylor gave about sixty acres at the forks of Brashears Creek and the Salt River for a town, which was named Taylorsville for him.
bodyMarkdown:
Taylorsville grew up where Brashears Creek flows into the Salt River, in the hill country southeast of Louisville. It is the county seat of Spencer County and a small city of about 1,250 people. Its story follows the slow shift from a frontier land grant to a county town.

## Richard Taylor's land

[Taylorsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylorsville,_Kentucky) was founded in 1799 on land belonging to Richard Taylor, a [Virginia native who ran a grist mill nearby](https://history.ky.gov/markers/taylorsville). At the time the site was part of Shelby County. On Taylor's own motion, the Shelby County Court took roughly 60 acres of his tract for a town, which was soon named for him.

The town site lay at the forks of Brashears Creek and the Salt River. It was formally admitted to record by the Shelby County Court in 1814.

## A new county

The Salt River country filled with farms in the early 1800s, and people far from the old county seats wanted courts closer to home. The 32nd Kentucky General Assembly formed [Spencer County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_County,_Kentucky) in January 1824 from parts of Bullitt, Shelby and Nelson counties. It became Kentucky's 77th county.

The new county was named for Capt. Spier Spencer, a Kentuckian who was killed at the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811. In December 1824 Taylorsville was chosen as the county seat, and the town was incorporated in 1829. Other Salt River stories include [Shepherdsville](/stories/shepherdsville-on-salt-river/) and [McAfee Station](/stories/mcafee-station-on-the-salt-river/).

## The Civil War's last months

Spencer County saw guerrilla violence near the end of the Civil War. Confederate guerrillas burned the courthouse at Taylorsville in January 1865, though the county's records were saved.

One account says the guerrilla leader William Quantrill was killed near the town in 1865. Another gives a fuller picture of [Quantrill's death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Quantrill). Union troops led by Edwin W. Terrell ambushed his band at Wakefield on May 10, 1865, and Quantrill was shot in the back and paralyzed. He was taken by wagon to a military prison hospital in Louisville and died there on June 6, 1865, at age 27.

## A lake on the Salt

In the 20th century the Salt River was dammed above the town. The Army Corps of Engineers began building the dam in 1974, and flooding began in 1983. The 3,050-acre [Taylorsville Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylorsville_Lake) runs about 18.5 miles and also reaches into Nelson and Anderson counties. It was built for flood control and recreation.

## Kentucky today

Taylorsville had 1,256 people in 2020, and Spencer County is now part of the Louisville metropolitan area. The lake, named for the town, is a major draw for fishing and boating, and Taylorsville Lake State Park sits on its northern shore. Shelby County towns such as [Shelbyville](/stories/shelbyville/) are a short drive north.
